summary:
Allwork.Space reports that US commercial real estate transaction activity accelerated in the first half of 2026, citing Green Street data. Sales of larger commercial properties (valued at $25 million or more) reached $164 billion between January and June, up nearly 30% from $126 billion in the first half of 2025. Smaller property transactions, in the $5 million to $25 million range, totaled $57.1 billion, a 9.3% increase over $52.3 billion a year earlier. Deals involving a sell-side adviser grew fastest, up 39.3% year over year. Green Street compiled the figures from roughly 40 brokerages plus property records, published reports and press releases.

Financing conditions have loosened somewhat. Major banks have expanded CRE lending, with Goldman Sachs issuing $40 billion in commercial real estate loans in the second quarter, a 21% year-over-year increase, per BisNow.

Two drivers stand out. First, construction of AI data centers has become a significant source of transaction and financing activity as large financial institutions seek exposure to the sector. Second, distress: office buildings hit by reduced post-pandemic demand and properties facing loan maturities continue to trade as owners and lenders work through higher borrowing costs.

The rate environment remains a constraint. The Federal Reserve has held its benchmark rate unchanged for five consecutive meetings, keeping pressure on financing costs even as deal volume improves. Some investors are actively hunting opportunities created by distressed sales and discounted assets.

Green Street's midyear read is that buyers and sellers are becoming more active while staying cautious about the broader economy. The piece is a market-level CRE investment story rather than a workplace operations story, with no coverage of workplace technology, occupancy tooling, or hybrid policy specifics beyond a passing reference to reduced office demand since the pandemic.
